_note: Every source Vigil draws on. 'checked' says how much of it the team actually read: 'full text', 'abstract', or 'summary' (a press release or a secondary page quoting it). 'status' is 'verified' when the figure was read in the source itself or its abstract, 'partly verified' when it was read only in a summary, and 'not used yet' when the source is listed for later work. Retrieved 2026-11-11.

sources.title: NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief: Design for Ionizing Radiation Protection (OCHMO-TB-020, Rev E, 2022)
sources.publisher: NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer
sources.gives: Career effective dose under 600 mSv for all ages and sexes [V1 4030]. Each solar particle event held under 250 mSv, measured against the October 1989 events [V1 4031]. Nuclear power sources under 20 mSv per mission year [V1 4032].
sources.used_for: The career limit on the Radiation screen and the per-storm limit.

sources.title: NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief: Carbon Dioxide
sources.publisher: NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer
sources.gives: Cabin CO2 limited to a one-hour average of 3 mmHg [V2 6004]. Headaches reported between 2.8 and 4.5 mmHg. 0.5% CO2 is 3.8 mmHg.
sources.used_for: Listed for a future cabin air signal. Vigil does not track CO2 yet.

sources.title: Zeitlin et al. 2013, Measurements of energetic particle radiation in transit to Mars on the Mars Science Laboratory, Science 340:1080
sources.publisher: Science (via the DLR repository and the SwRI press release)
sources.gives: About 1.8 mSv per day during cruise, mostly from galactic cosmic rays. 0.66 plus or minus 0.12 Sv for the shortest round trip with current propulsion.
sources.used_for: The background dose rate in the simulated cruise (76 uSv per hour, about 1.8 mSv per day).

sources.title: Hassler et al. 2014, Curiosity RAD measurements on the surface of Mars, Science
sources.publisher: Science (via NBC News and Space.com reporting)
sources.gives: About 0.64 mSv per day on the Martian surface, roughly a third of the cruise rate.
sources.used_for: Reference figure for surface stays. Not yet used in a simulated phase.

sources.title: Simonsen et al., NASA ASCEND presentation draft (NTRS 20250006168)
sources.gives: ISS effective dose of about 0.2 to 0.5 mSv per day, about 40 to 90 mSv over six months.
sources.used_for: Comparison on the About screen. The simulated mission is a Mars cruise, not the ISS.

sources.title: Solar Proton Events Affecting the Earth Environment, 1976 to present
sources.publisher: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, hosted by NOAA NCEI
sources.gives: 318 events with start time, peak time, and peak >10 MeV proton flux in pfu. The largest are March 1991 (43,500 pfu) and October 1989 (42,200 pfu).
sources.used_for: The day-120 storm replays the 19 October 1989 event: its 27-hour rise and its size. Bundled in data/space_weather and refreshed with scripts/fetch_space_weather.py.

sources.title: DONKI Space Weather Database, solar energetic particle events
sources.gives: SEP events since 2010 with linked flares and coronal mass ejections, as JSON.
sources.used_for: Not downloaded: the CCMC servers did not answer from our network, and the public NASA API limits each request to 60 days.

sources.title: Meta-analysis of 25 studies of bone loss in space travelers, npj Microgravity, 2020 (doi 10.1038/s41526-020-0103-2)
sources.gives: Bone loss of about 1 to 1.5 percent per month in long flights, only partly helped by non-drug countermeasures. Individual studies range from 0.4 to 1.8 percent per month.
sources.used_for: The slow downward trend of the bone marker index: about 7.5 percent over 180 days.

sources.title: What happens to bones in space?
sources.gives: Astronauts lose on average 1 to 2 percent of bone mineral density each month in microgravity.
sources.used_for: Cross-check for the bone trend.

sources.title: NASA ISS exercise prescription (NASA podcast and presentations)
sources.gives: 2.5 hours a day, 6 days a week scheduled for exercise on the ISS, including setup. A 2024 Phys.org report puts the average at about 2 hours a day.
sources.used_for: The crew's usual resistive exercise time: 120 minutes a day.

sources.title: Dodds et al. 2014, Grip strength across the life course: normative data from twelve British studies, PLoS ONE 9:e113637
sources.gives: Peak median grip strength of 51 kg in men (ages 29 to 39) and 31 kg in women (ages 26 to 42), from 49,964 people.
sources.used_for: The crew's grip strength baselines: mean 41 kg, spread 10 kg, for a mixed crew.

sources.title: Mackowiak et al. 1992, study of normal body temperature in 148 healthy adults, JAMA
sources.gives: Mean oral temperature 36.8 C in healthy adults, upper limit of normal 37.7 C, daily swing of about 0.5 C.
sources.used_for: The crew's temperature baselines (mean 36.8 C) and the usual-range note.

sources.title: Pearson et al. 2003, AHA/CDC scientific statement on markers of inflammation, Circulation
sources.gives: hsCRP risk bands: below 1 mg/L low, 1 to 3 average, above 3 high. A secondary summary adds that values above 10 mg/L usually have an acute cause.
sources.used_for: The CRP usual range and the 10 mg/L hard limit.

sources.title: Interleukin-6 reference intervals: Mayo Clinic Laboratories and Said et al. 2021 meta-analysis (J Med Virol)
sources.publisher: Mayo Clinic Laboratories; Journal of Medical Virology
sources.gives: Mayo reference interval below 6.4 pg/mL. The meta-analysis of 140 studies gives a pooled healthy-adult mean of 5.19 pg/mL. Upper limits differ between labs and assays.
sources.used_for: The IL-6 usual range note.

sources.title: Blood differential test
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus, US National Library of Medicine
sources.gives: Lymphocytes are 20 to 40 percent of white blood cells (archived copy of the page).
sources.used_for: The lymphocyte ratio usual range (0.20 to 0.40).

sources.title: Crucian et al. 2018, Immune system dysregulation during spaceflight, Frontiers in Immunology 9:1437
sources.gives: Immune dysregulation and reactivation of latent herpesviruses persist across six-month orbital missions. Adaptive immunity is reduced and some innate responses are raised.
sources.used_for: Why the simulated mission includes an immune stress event. It gives no event size, so the size is the team's.

sources.title: Garrett-Bakelman et al. 2019, The NASA Twins Study, Science
sources.gives: Signs of inflammation in flight, telomere lengthening in flight, and some changes lasting more than six months after landing. A study of one person.
sources.used_for: Background for the immune system. Vigil uses no Twins Study data.

sources.title: Normal resting heart rate for adults
sources.gives: 60 to 100 bpm awake at rest for adults. Athletes can sit in the 40s or 50s.
sources.used_for: The resting heart rate usual range. Crew baselines sit low in it, as for fit adults.

sources.title: Shaffer and Ginsberg 2017, An overview of heart rate variability metrics and norms, Frontiers in Public Health 5:258 (Table 6, short-term norms from Nunan et al.)
sources.gives: Short-term (about 5 minute) RMSSD in healthy adults: mean 42 ms, SD 15, range 19 to 75 ms.
sources.used_for: The crew's HRV baselines: mean 42 ms, spread 15 ms.

sources.title: 2017 ACC/AHA high blood pressure guideline (Whelton et al.)
sources.publisher: American Heart Association and American College of Cardiology
sources.gives: Normal below 120/80 mmHg. Stage 1 hypertension 130 to 139 or 80 to 89. Stage 2 at 140/90 or higher.
sources.used_for: The blood pressure usual ranges. The hard limits (160/100) are the team's.

sources.title: 2015 Heart Rhythm Society consensus on postural tachycardia, as reviewed in PMC6113123
sources.gives: A sustained heart rate rise of at least 30 bpm within 10 minutes of standing defines postural tachycardia in adults.
sources.used_for: The upper end of the standing heart rate rise range.

sources.title: Pulse oximetry
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus, US National Library of Medicine
sources.gives: Normal oxygen saturation is 95 to 100 percent.
sources.used_for: The blood oxygen usual range.

sources.title: Barger et al. 2014, ten-year study of astronaut sleep, Lancet Neurology
sources.publisher: Lancet Neurology (via Brigham and Women's Hospital release)
sources.gives: Astronauts slept 5.96 hours a night on shuttle missions and 6.09 on the ISS, against 8.5 scheduled. 64 astronauts on 80 shuttle missions and 21 on 13 ISS missions, by wrist actigraphy.
sources.used_for: The crew's sleep baselines: mean 6.1 hours.

sources.title: Basner et al. 2013, Mars 520-d mission simulation reveals protracted crew hypokinesis and alterations of sleep duration and timing, PNAS
sources.gives: Over 520 days of isolation the crew grew more sedentary, and sleep timing and length changed. People differed widely.
sources.used_for: Why the behavioral slide lowers sleep and social contact together. Event size is the team's.

sources.title: HI-SEAS crews, Frontiers in Physiology 2022 (fphys.2022.898841)
sources.gives: 18 people across three 8 to 12 month simulated Mars missions, tracked with wearables, hair and urine markers and self-ratings. Problems were most likely after the halfway point.
sources.used_for: The behavioral slide starts on day 90, the halfway point of the 180-day mission.

sources.title: SIRIUS isolation missions (17 days, 4 months, 8 months) at IBMP, Moscow
sources.gives: Study plans for immune function, salivary cytokines and herpesvirus reactivation in 4 and 8 month isolation. No published outcomes found.
sources.used_for: Not used: no results to draw on yet.

sources.title: NASA CHAPEA Mission 1 (378 days, June 2023 to July 2024)
sources.gives: A four-person crew lived 378 days in a simulated Mars habitat with a one-way message delay of up to 22 minutes. Health results are not published yet.
sources.used_for: Supports the 20-minute one-way delay used for Earth packets.

sources.title: Inspiration4 mission data in NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSD-569, 570, 571, 575 for blood)
sources.gives: De-identified blood counts, metabolic panels, cytokines and multi-omics from four commercial astronauts.
sources.used_for: Not imported. These are records of real people, and the project rule is to use none. The import format can read OSDR-style tables if the team decides otherwise.

sources.title: OSDR Biological Data API
sources.gives: Programmatic access to GeneLab and ALSDA data and metadata.
sources.used_for: Not used yet.

sources.title: Apple Health export (export.xml)
sources.publisher: Apple, format described by independent guides
sources.gives: Readings stored as Record elements with type, unit, value and startDate. Apple publishes no schema, so the format is read from real exports.
sources.used_for: Vigil can import resting heart rate, blood oxygen, temperature, blood pressure and sleep from an Apple Health export.
